headline: High-risk default data leakage and cascading errors: LangGraph’s broad egress and filesystem/tool access can expose IoT data and amplify EMQX outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: EMQX exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress, while LangGraph can read/write files, run browsers, and execute developer-defined tools. No shared channel is documented, so direct injection is not proven; however, if EMQX output is bridged into LangGraph via files or API payloads, prompt-like content could be misread as instructions.
conditions: IF EMQX outputs are copied into LangGraph prompts or tool inputs without sanitization
IF a shared file or API payload is used as the bridge between the two agents
mitigations: Add a strict delimiter and schema validator for any EMQX-to-LangGraph handoff
Disable automatic ingestion of raw API responses into prompts
Review one sample handoff for instruction-like text before enabling automation

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; LangGraph reads and writes application-defined files and sends data to model providers and developer-defined tools. A shared workspace or checkpointer could move IoT data into LangGraph’s context and then out to third parties. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default deployments, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF EMQX data is stored in a shared workspace or checkpointer accessible to LangGraph
IF LangGraph forwards that state to model providers or external tools
mitigations: Separate EMQX and LangGraph storage locations
Redact IoT payloads before they enter LangGraph state
Restrict LangGraph tools to non-production endpoints for a quick test run
Audit one persisted state record for sensitive fields

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX can make HTTP API calls and has broad egress; LangGraph can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write files. If both operate on the same mutable workspace or shared state store, they can overwrite each other’s artifacts or race on state. The profiles do not show locking, so conflict risk is real but bounded.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or checkpointer namespace
IF EMQX API-driven updates and LangGraph file writes target the same mutable resource
mitigations: Assign separate directories or namespaces for each agent
Turn on a single-writer convention for shared state
Run a quick concurrency smoke test with two simultaneous updates

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is a stateful orchestration layer that can treat upstream outputs as node inputs and trigger tools or subprocesses; EMQX can emit IoT-facing data over HTTP APIs. If EMQX output is fed into LangGraph without verification, LangGraph may propagate incorrect facts into downstream actions. Because the pair can automate actions and the profiles do not show a verification gate, the blast radius is potentially broad.
conditions: IF LangGraph consumes EMQX output as authoritative node input
IF downstream LangGraph nodes trigger external actions based on that input
mitigations: Insert a human review step before any action-taking node
Require schema validation on EMQX outputs
Log one end-to-end run and inspect for unverified assumptions
Disable action nodes until the data path is tested

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while LangGraph handles model-provider API keys and application-defined state with broad egress. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if IoT data or regulated records flow into LangGraph’s external model calls or persistent checkpointer. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their interaction.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is stored in LangGraph state or sent to model providers
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the shared checkpointer
mitigations: Classify the IoT data before routing it into LangGraph
Set a short retention window on the checkpointer
Confirm the model provider region for one test run
Document which data classes are allowed in shared state
